Due process similarly has affected interpretation of statutes governing 
notice in immigration proceedings. In Pereira v. Sessiorbs, 585 U.S. 198 (2018), 
the Supreme Court considered the case of a noncitizen who had been found 
inehgible for cancellation of removal because he had been served a notice to 
appear without time and date information, which the immigration court had 
found stopped the accrual of continuous physical presence. The Court reversed, 
holding that a putative notice to appear lacking specific time or place 
inform A tinn is not in fact a notice to appear at all. As the Court explained, 
“[flailing to specify integral information Eke the time and place of removal 
proceedings unquestionably would deprive the notice to appear of its essential 
character.” Id. at 214 (quotation omitted). Therefore, “[a] putative notice to 
appear that fails to designate the specific time or place of the noncitizen’s 
removal proceedings is not a ‘notice to appear under section 1229(a)’ ” at all. 
Id. at 208—09. In Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 144 S. Ct. 1637 (2024), the 
Supreme Court held that a single-document notice is not required. Under 
§ 1229 (a)(l)-(2), “notice to appear” is provided when an initial, incomplete 
document and a later amendment together provide the required information. 
Id. at 1647-49.
